stops.name: The Vittoriale, the gift of the shrine to the Italian people
stops.campa: By deed of December 1923 he donates the Vittoriale, and himself with it, to the Italian people: the house, the relics, the manuscripts, the future mausoleum, all made national while the donor still lives in it, editing his own reliquary. Over the entrance he sets the motto of the whole economy of his life: I have what I have given. The state accepts, and thereby ratifies the doctrine: that the nation is the heir, and the poet's biography is public property, a gospel in objects.
stops.quote: Io ho quel che ho donato.
stops.quote_source: Motto inscribed at the entrance of the Vittoriale

stops.name: The Vittoriale, Principe di Montenevoso
stops.campa: When Fiume is at last annexed to Italy in 1924, the King raises the poet to the rank of prince: Principe di Montenevoso, prince of the Snowy Mountain, the peak that marks the new eastern border. The title is a treaty written as heraldry: the state paying its debt to the man who made the border imaginable. He, who began as the notary's grandson of Pescara and styled himself duke in a newspaper, ends in the almanac of the nobility by act of parliament, ennobled for a city he took against the government's orders.

stops.name: The Vittoriale, Mussolini comes as a pilgrim
stops.campa: The Duce comes up the hill to the poet, not the poet down to Rome. Mussolini is received among the relics, shown the flag of Randaccio, and conducted through rooms arranged like the stations of a private religion. The two seducers of crowds measure each other with perfect courtesy and perfect mistrust. Mussolini departs having paid for everything and secured one thing: that the archangel will thunder only from his own hill. The canon keeps the visit as the meeting of the church and the state of the Italian myth, and leaves delicately unsaid which was which.

stops.name: The Vittoriale, the prow of the Puglia set in the hillside
stops.campa: The Navy gives him the cruiser Puglia, the ship of the Adriatic vigils, whose captain was killed at Split, and he has her bow carried up the hill in pieces and rebuilt jutting from the cypresses, prow aimed across Garda toward the Adriatic she can no longer reach. A warship run aground in a garden, crewed by memory: no emblem of the mutilated victory could be more literal, and none more serene. Above her he hangs the SVA of Vienna in the auditorium, and moors the MAS of Buccari below: the whole war, dry-docked in paradise.

stops.name: The Vittoriale, Il libro segreto, the last mask
stops.campa: Old now, sleepless on cocaine and memory, he publishes under the mask of Angelo Cocles the Cento e cento e cento e cento pagine del libro segreto: the hundred and hundred and hundred and hundred pages of the secret book of Gabriele d'Annunzio tempted to die. The prose breaks into fragments, confession, and night-thoughts: the inventor of the inimitable life files its final inventory. The dandy, the Comandante, the prince recede; what remains at the desk is a lucid, half-blind old craftsman of Italian, testing whether the language can still lift.

stops.name: Verona, the station, the last warning to Mussolini
stops.campa: September 1937: Mussolini returns by rail from the German triumph, and the old poet comes down from his hill to meet the train at Verona. On the platform, the last encounter: d'Annunzio urges him against binding Italy to Hitler, the Germany he has long mocked in his letters, and pleads the old Latin sea against the new northern axis. The Duce embraces him, promises nothing, and steams south. It is the final public act of the Comandante: a prophecy delivered in a railway station, unheeded, and, the canon notes, exact.

stops.name: The Vittoriale, death at the writing desk in the Zambracca
stops.campa: On 1 March 1938, at 8:05 in the evening, seated at the little desk of the Zambracca where he answered letters and kept his medicines, the poet's head drops to the wood: cerebral hemorrhage, instant. He dies writing: the one death, of all the deaths he drafted for himself since the horse on the road to Francavilla, that needed no press release. The lake is dark under the window. Mussolini orders state mourning; the telegrams call him the John the Baptist of the regime, and the family knows he would have corrected the theology and kept the capital letters.

stops.name: The mausoleum above the lake, the Comandante among his legionaries
stops.campa: They bury him on the hill with a state funeral, and later raise over him the mausoleum he had planned: three concentric rings of stone on the highest terrace, the tombs of ten legionaries of Fiume in a circle and the Comandante lifted at the centre, above the cypresses, above the Puglia's prow, above the water. From the summit the whole of Garda lies open to the south: Goethe's lake and his, the German pilgrim's road and the Italian archangel's roost, one water. The journey that began on a river-port in the Abruzzo ends in white stone in the air: the life, as promised, inimitable.
